title: Azure Monitor: Metrics, Logs & Log Analytics
summary: How Azure Monitor collects metrics and logs, how diagnostic settings and agents route data, and how to query it with KQL and Insights.
overview: Azure Monitor is the unified monitoring platform for Azure, on-premises and other clouds. It stores two fundamental data types: metrics (numeric time series, near real time, lightweight) and logs (rich, structured records queried with Kusto Query Language in a Log Analytics workspace).

Platform metrics are collected automatically for most resources. Resource logs (diagnostic logs) are not — you create diagnostic settings to send them to a Log Analytics workspace, a storage account, Event Hubs or a partner solution. The Activity log records subscription-level control-plane events (who created, changed or deleted what).

Inside VMs, the Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) collects guest OS performance counters, event logs and syslog according to data collection rules (DCRs). Curated Insights (VM insights, Storage insights, Network insights) provide ready-made workbooks.

keyConcepts.definition: Numeric values sampled at regular intervals (e.g., CPU %). Explored in Metrics Explorer; platform metrics retained for 93 days.
Records with many properties, stored in tables in a Log Analytics workspace and queried with KQL.
The data store and query environment for logs; has region, retention and access-control settings.
Subscription-level log of management operations and service health events. Kept 90 days by default; send it to a workspace for longer retention and querying.
Routes a resource's platform logs and metrics to destinations. Configured per resource (or at scale with Policy).
Current agent for collecting guest data from VMs; replaces the legacy Log Analytics agent (MMA), which was retired in August 2024.
Defines what data AMA collects and where it's sent.
Read-only query language: Table | where … | summarize … by … | render timechart.
Curated monitoring experiences such as VM insights (performance and dependency map), Storage insights and Network insights.

howItWorks: Resources emit platform metrics automatically; view them in Metrics Explorer with aggregation (avg, max, min, sum, count) and splitting by dimension.
Create diagnostic settings on resources to send resource logs to a Log Analytics workspace (and/or storage, Event Hubs).
Install AMA on VMs and associate DCRs to collect guest performance counters and logs; enable VM insights for curated views.
Query logs in Log Analytics with KQL, pin results to dashboards or workbooks, and create log search alerts.
Use the Activity log to audit who did what at the control plane.
whenToUse: Metrics for fast, numeric alerting and charts (CPU, latency, transactions).
Logs for troubleshooting, correlation across resources, and security/audit analysis.
Storage account destinations for cheap long-term archive; Event Hubs to stream to SIEMs or third-party tools.
VM insights to see performance trends and process dependencies across VMs.
examTips: Resource logs aren't collected until you create a diagnostic setting — the fix for 'logs are missing'.
'Who deleted the VM?' → Activity log.
Guest OS metrics (e.g., memory inside the VM) require an agent (AMA) — host metrics don't include guest memory usage.
Retain logs for years cheaply → archive to a storage account, or configure workspace retention/archive.
Stream logs to a third-party SIEM → Event Hubs destination.
Know basic KQL: where filters rows, summarize aggregates, project picks columns, order by sorts, ago() for time.
commonMistakes: Expecting resource logs to appear without a diagnostic setting.
Installing the retired Log Analytics agent for new deployments instead of AMA.
Using metrics when the question needs detailed per-request records (logs).

confusedWith.name: Metrics vs logs
confusedWith.difference: Metrics are numeric time series; logs are structured event records queried with KQL.

confusedWith.name: Application Insights
confusedWith.difference: Application Insights is the APM feature of Azure Monitor for app telemetry (requests, dependencies, exceptions).

title: Alerts, Action Groups & Alert Processing Rules
summary: Create metric, log search and activity log alerts, notify and automate with action groups, and suppress or route alerts with processing rules.
overview: Azure Monitor alerts proactively notify you when conditions in your monitoring data are met. An alert rule combines a scope (resources), a condition (signal + logic) and actions.

Action groups are reusable collections of notifications (email, SMS, push, voice) and actions (Azure Function, Logic App, Automation runbook, webhook, ITSM, Event Hubs). Many alert rules can share one action group.
Alert processing rules modify fired alerts at scale: suppress notifications during a maintenance window, or add an action group to every alert in a subscription — without editing each rule.

keyConcepts.definition: Evaluates a metric at a frequency against a static or dynamic threshold. Near real time; stateful (resolves automatically).
Runs a KQL query on a schedule and fires on results (e.g., count > 0).
Fires on control-plane events (e.g., a VM deleted, a policy operation) or service health / resource health events.
Machine-learned threshold based on historical behavior, useful for seasonal patterns.
Sev 0 (Critical) to Sev 4 (Verbose).
Notification and action targets; regional or global resource reusable across alert rules.
Applies to fired alerts in a scope to suppress actions (e.g., maintenance windows) or add action groups.
Monitor condition (Fired/Resolved) set by the system; user response (New/Acknowledged/Closed) set by people.

howItWorks: Create an alert rule: choose scope, signal (metric, log query, activity log), condition and evaluation frequency.
Attach one or more action groups and set severity and details.
When the condition is met the alert fires, creating an alert instance and triggering the action groups.
Alert processing rules evaluated on the fired alert can suppress actions or add action groups.
Manage alerts in the Alerts blade; acknowledge and close them as you respond.
whenToUse: Metric alerts for performance thresholds (CPU, available memory, latency).
Log search alerts for patterns across logs (failed sign-ins, error events, missing heartbeats).
Activity log alerts for critical administrative actions or Service Health incidents.
Alert processing rules for planned maintenance to avoid noisy notifications.
examTips: 'Notify the on-call team by SMS and email when CPU > 85%' → metric alert + action group with SMS and email.
'Run a script automatically when the alert fires' → action group with an Automation runbook, Azure Function or Logic App.
'No notifications during Saturday maintenance' → alert processing rule with a suppression schedule — not deleting/disabling every rule.
'Alert when someone deletes a resource' → activity log alert.
One action group can be reused by many alert rules — minimize administrative effort.
commonMistakes: Disabling alert rules for maintenance instead of using a processing rule.
Creating separate notification settings in every rule instead of a shared action group.
Using a metric alert for something only visible in logs.

confusedWith.name: Budget alerts
confusedWith.difference: Cost Management budgets alert on spending, not resource telemetry (though they can use action groups).

confusedWith.name: Service Health
confusedWith.difference: Service Health reports Azure platform issues; activity log alerts on Service Health events notify you of them.

title: Network Watcher & Connection Monitor
summary: Diagnose and monitor Azure networking with IP flow verify, next hop, connection troubleshoot, packet capture, flow logs and Connection Monitor.
overview: Azure Network Watcher is a regional set of tools to monitor, diagnose and log IaaS networking. It's enabled automatically per region when you create a VNet.

Diagnostic tools answer specific questions: Is this traffic allowed? (IP flow verify, NSG diagnostics) Where does this traffic go? (next hop) Can A reach B, and why not? (connection troubleshoot) What exactly is on the wire? (packet capture).

Monitoring features track connectivity and traffic over time: Connection Monitor measures reachability and latency between endpoints, and flow logs record IP traffic for analysis with Traffic Analytics.

keyConcepts.definition: Checks whether a packet (5-tuple) to/from a VM is allowed or denied, and names the NSG rule responsible.
Evaluates traffic against all applicable NSGs and shows the result per NSG and rule.
Shows the next hop type and IP for traffic from a VM to a destination, and the route table responsible.
Tests a one-time connection from a VM to a VM, FQDN, URI or IP and reports hops, latency and issues.
Continuous monitoring of connectivity, latency and packet loss between Azure and on-premises endpoints, with alerts.
Captures traffic on a VM (via the Network Watcher extension) to storage or a local file.
Log IP traffic. VNet flow logs are the replacement for NSG flow logs, which are being retired.
Processes flow logs in Log Analytics to visualize traffic patterns and threats.
Visual map of resources in a VNet and their relationships.

howItWorks: Network Watcher is enabled per region (in the NetworkWatcherRG resource group by default).
Run diagnostic tools on demand from the portal, CLI or PowerShell, targeting a VM/NIC.
Create a Connection Monitor with source endpoints (which use the agent/extension), destinations and test configurations; results flow to Log Analytics and can trigger alerts.
Enable flow logs to a storage account, and optionally Traffic Analytics into a Log Analytics workspace.
whenToUse: 'VM can't be reached on port 443' → IP flow verify / NSG diagnostics.
'Traffic isn't going through the firewall' → next hop.
'Is the app server reachable from the web server, and where does it fail?' → connection troubleshoot.
'Alert if latency to on-premises exceeds 100 ms' → Connection Monitor.
Auditing and analyzing traffic flows → flow logs + Traffic Analytics.
examTips: IP flow verify tells you allow/deny and which NSG rule; next hop tells you routing. Pick the tool that matches the symptom.
Connection Monitor is for continuous monitoring over time; connection troubleshoot is a one-time test.
Packet capture requires the Network Watcher VM extension.
Network Watcher is regional — it must exist in the region of the resources you diagnose.
New NSG flow logs can no longer be created; use VNet flow logs.
commonMistakes: Using next hop to diagnose an NSG block (or IP flow verify to diagnose routing).
Expecting connection troubleshoot to keep monitoring over time.
Forgetting that flow logs need a storage account in the same region.

confusedWith.name: Azure Monitor metrics
confusedWith.difference: Metrics show aggregated resource numbers; Network Watcher tools diagnose specific flows and paths.

confusedWith.name: Effective security rules
confusedWith.difference: Shows all NSG rules applied to a NIC; IP flow verify tests a specific flow against them.

versionNote: NSG flow logs are on a retirement path in favor of VNet flow logs; check current dates on Microsoft Learn.

title: Azure Backup: Vaults, Policies & Restores
summary: Protect VMs, file shares, disks, blobs and on-premises data with Recovery Services and Backup vaults, policies, restores, reports and alerts.
overview: Azure Backup is a managed service for backing up and restoring data in Azure and on-premises. There's no backup infrastructure to deploy for Azure workloads — you create a vault, define a policy and enable protection.

Two vault types exist. Recovery Services vaults protect Azure VMs, SQL Server and SAP HANA in VMs, Azure Files, and on-premises files via the MARS agent (and servers via MABS/DPM). Backup vaults protect newer workloads such as Azure Disks, Azure Blobs, Azure Database for PostgreSQL and AKS.
Backup policies define when backups run and how long recovery points are kept. Soft delete and immutability protect backups from accidental or malicious deletion.

keyConcepts.definition: Vault for Azure VMs, SQL/SAP HANA in VMs, Azure Files, MARS agent and MABS/DPM backups.
Vault for Azure Disks, Blobs, PostgreSQL, AKS and other newer data sources.
Schedule (daily/hourly for enhanced VM policy) and retention for daily, weekly, monthly and yearly points.
Snapshots retained locally for fast restores before/alongside transfer to the vault tier.
LRS, ZRS or GRS. Set it before protecting any items — it can't be changed afterwards.
With a GRS vault, restore data in the paired secondary region.
Deleted backup data is retained (14 days by default) so it can be recovered.
Microsoft Azure Recovery Services agent; backs up files, folders and system state from Windows machines directly to a Recovery Services vault.
Built on Log Analytics; require diagnostic settings on the vault to send data to a workspace.

howItWorks: Create a vault in the same region as the resources you protect and set its storage redundancy.
Configure a backup policy (schedule and retention), or use the default.
Enable backup on items — for VMs, Azure installs a backup extension and takes snapshots.
Recovery points are kept per policy; restore by creating a new VM, restoring disks, replacing existing disks, or recovering individual files.
Monitor jobs and alerts in Backup center / Business Continuity Center and configure reports via diagnostic settings to Log Analytics.
whenToUse: Protect against accidental deletion, corruption and ransomware with point-in-time recovery.
Long-term retention for compliance (monthly/yearly points).
Backing up on-premises Windows files and folders to Azure with MARS.
Restoring individual files from a VM backup without restoring the whole VM.
examTips: The vault must be in the same region as the Azure VMs you back up.
Choose the vault's storage redundancy (e.g., GRS for Cross Region Restore) before protecting items.
Azure Disks and Blobs → Backup vault. Azure VMs, Azure Files, MARS → Recovery Services vault.
File-level restore from a VM backup mounts the recovery point via a script — no full VM restore needed.
Backups are not disaster recovery replication: restoring takes longer than an Azure Site Recovery failover.
You can't delete a vault that still contains protected items or soft-deleted data.
commonMistakes: Creating a vault in a different region from the VMs.
Trying to change vault redundancy after items are protected.
Confusing Backup (restore data to a point in time) with Site Recovery (fail over running workloads).
Expecting backup reports to work without configuring diagnostic settings to Log Analytics.

confusedWith.name: Azure Site Recovery
confusedWith.difference: ASR replicates VMs continuously for failover (low RPO/RTO); Backup keeps point-in-time copies for restore.

confusedWith.name: Storage redundancy
confusedWith.difference: GRS on a storage account replicates data (including deletes); Backup keeps historical recovery points.

title: Azure Site Recovery
summary: Replicate VMs to a secondary region, run test failovers, fail over and fail back to keep workloads running during regional outages.
overview: Azure Site Recovery (ASR) is a disaster recovery (DR) service. It continuously replicates workloads — Azure VMs between regions, or on-premises VMware, Hyper-V and physical servers to Azure — so you can fail over when the primary site goes down.
Recovery plans orchestrate failover of multi-tier apps in order, with scripts and manual steps. Test failovers validate DR without impacting production or replication.
Where Azure Backup answers 'restore my data to last Tuesday', Site Recovery answers 'keep my application running in another region within minutes'.

keyConcepts.definition: Recovery point objective — how much data loss is acceptable (time since last recovery point).
Recovery time objective — how quickly the workload must be running again.
Recovery point retention and app-consistent snapshot frequency.
Groups machines and defines failover order, scripts and manual actions.
Creates VMs in an isolated network from a recovery point to validate DR; production keeps running. Clean up afterwards.
Starts VMs in the target region; commit finalizes the chosen recovery point.
After failover, reverse replication and later fail back to the original region.
Storage in the source region that temporarily holds changes before they're sent to the target (for Azure-to-Azure).

howItWorks: Create (or let ASR create) a Recovery Services vault in the target region.
Enable replication on VMs, choosing the target region, resource group, network and replication policy. ASR installs the Mobility service extension on Azure VMs.
Initial replication copies disks; then changes replicate continuously.
Run a test failover into an isolated VNet to validate, then clean it up.
During an outage, fail over (via a recovery plan), commit, then re-protect and eventually fail back.
whenToUse: Business-critical workloads that must survive a regional outage with low RTO/RPO.
Migrating on-premises or cross-region workloads with minimal downtime.
Regular DR drills required by compliance (test failover).
examTips: 'Validate DR without impacting production' → test failover into an isolated network.
'Fail over multiple VMs in a specific order' → recovery plan.
'Keep an app running if the region fails' → Site Recovery, not Backup.
For Azure-to-Azure, the vault is created in the target (secondary) region, not the source.
Choose a target region that's different from the source; commonly the paired region.
commonMistakes: Using Azure Backup to meet a low-RTO DR requirement.
Running a test failover into the production VNet.
Forgetting to clean up after a test failover.

confusedWith.name: Azure Backup
confusedWith.difference: Backup = point-in-time restore of data; ASR = replication and failover of running workloads.

confusedWith.name: Availability zones
confusedWith.difference: Zones protect within a region; ASR protects against loss of a whole region.
